_what: Crocodile born-as long-form, written to the dog / lion v2 structure and Social Studio's 11/15 long-form rule: promise by 0:05, no rules or score intro, no silent countdowns, a timed shot every 2 to 4 s (test), one mid-video pick-a-number comment prompt, citations on screen (source_tag) and in the description only. Lead species: saltwater crocodile (C. porosus). Facts: /workspace/drafts/facts/crocodile-bornas.md (CB1 to CB55).
titles: Your Life as a Crocodile: 8 Things You Have to Get Through
_titles_note: Title from the pipeline pitch, concept 5, and this brief. 'Sucks' stays out. Single title, no A/B set.

lines.say: You were just born a crocodile. Here are eight things you have to get through.
lines.vis: Frame 0: saltwater crocodile hatchling cracking an egg in a vegetation mound; narration on it at 0.0 s / Eight numbered tiles slam in face down around the egg; title card lands

shots.vis: Frame 0: saltwater crocodile hatchling cracking an egg in a vegetation mound; narration on it at 0.0 s
Eight numbered tiles slam in face down around the egg; title card lands

lines.say: You're a saltwater crocodile, about seventy grams, and about thirty centimetres long.
lines.vis: Push in on the wet hatchling, about hand-length / Chip: ABOUT 70 G / ABOUT 30 CM

shots.vis: Push in on the wet hatchling, about hand-length; then Chip: ABOUT 70 G / ABOUT 30 CM

lines.say: Your first job is to get out of a mound of vegetation, close to the water.

lines.say: Number one. The nest.
lines.vis: Voiced number card whips in over the mound (no silent hold)

shots.vis: Voiced number card whips in over the mound (no silent hold)

lines.say: Your mother builds a mound of vegetation and soil along a watercourse, usually within ten metres of permanent water, so the eggs stay above flood levels.
lines.vis: Female saltwater crocodile scrapes plants and earth into a mound / Chip: USUALLY WITHIN 10 M OF WATER / Eggs set into the mound, above the waterline / Wide: the river close by

shots.vis: Female saltwater crocodile scrapes plants and earth into a mound
Chip: USUALLY WITHIN 10 M OF WATER
Eggs set into the mound, above the waterline
Wide: the river close by

lines.say: Embryos breathe through the shell, and they drown if the nest is flooded.
lines.vis: Close on a shell; tiny air-exchange marks / Floodwater climbing the mound / Meter dips toward RAW

shots.vis: Close on a shell; tiny air-exchange marks; then Floodwater climbing the mound
Meter dips toward RAW

lines.say: Meet the guy in the cardboard snout. That's Meatball. He's living all eight from the couch, with a rubber stamp.
lines.vis: Reveal: Meatball on the couch in a cardboard crocodile snout / Close on the snout, one tooth drawn on / He holds up a rubber stamp: RAW on one side, SWEET on the other

shots.vis: Reveal: Meatball on the couch in a cardboard crocodile snout
Close on the snout, one tooth drawn on
He holds up a rubber stamp: RAW on one side, SWEET on the other

shots.vis: Noodle in the doorway, wagging (name tag pops); then Sauce on the armrest, unimpressed (name tag pops)

shots.vis: Meatball stacks couch cushions into a messy mound; then Sauce hops on top and sits
The mound sags

lines.say: She lays about fifty eggs, in Australian counts, or anywhere from forty to seventy.

shots.vis: Eggs appear in the mound, counted up to about 50; then Range chip: 40 TO 70
Chip: AUSTRALIAN COUNTS

lines.say: Incubation is typically eighty to ninety days, depending on temperature.
lines.vis: Calendar pages flip across roughly three months / A temperature gauge beside the mound / Chip: TYPICALLY 80-90 DAYS

shots.vis: Calendar pages flip across roughly three months; then A temperature gauge beside the mound; then Chip: TYPICALLY 80-90 DAYS

lines.say: Thirty-two degrees Celsius produces both sexes, but most are male. Temperatures lower or higher produce more females. Very high or very low temperatures kill the embryos.
lines.vis: Thermometer settles on 32°C; male and female icons, more males / The needle drops, then climbs; female icons increase / The needle hits the far ends; those eggs fade

shots.vis: Thermometer settles on 32°C; male and female icons, more males
The needle drops, then climbs; female icons increase

lines.say: Throughout incubation, she protects the nest from predators, including other crocodiles, goannas, feral pigs and humans.
lines.vis: Mother stays by the mound / Silhouettes at the edge: a goanna, a pig, another crocodile / She holds her ground

shots.vis: Mother stays by the mound; then Silhouettes at the edge: a goanna, a pig, another crocodile
She holds her ground

lines.say: Meatball guarded his cushion nest. Noodle took a cushion. The nest got smaller.
lines.vis: Meatball sits beside the cushion pile / Noodle tugs a cushion away / The pile is one cushion shorter

lines.vis: Voiced number card over a hatching egg

shots.vis: Voiced number card over a hatching egg

lines.say: You can break out of the egg yourself. Squawking may bring your mother, who may dig you out. She may even roll unhatched eggs in her mouth to help them emerge.
lines.vis: Hatchling cracks the shell from inside / A chirp; the mother's head turns / She digs at the mound / An unhatched egg rolls gently in her mouth; a hatchling slides out

shots.vis: Hatchling cracks the shell from inside

shots.vis: Mother lifts a hatchling in her jaws, carefully
She walks it down to the water

lines.say: Hatchlings form a crèche and stay under her care for up to five weeks before they start to disperse.

shots.vis: Meatball picks up a sock in the cardboard snout; then Noodle tugs it free and trots off

lines.say: It is estimated that up to seventy-five percent of eggs laid in a season will not hatch, mostly from infertility, flooding, overheating, poor gas exchange and drying out, not from predators.
lines.vis: A grid of eggs; many fade for reasons other than a predator / Icons: flood, heat, dry air, a blank infertile cell / A goanna silhouette stays dim in the corner / Meter dips toward RAW

shots.vis: A grid of eggs; many fade for reasons other than a predator

A goanna silhouette stays dim in the corner
Meter dips toward RAW

lines.card: UP TO 75% OF EGGS DO NOT HATCH

lines.say: Northern Territory figures say, on average, only twenty-five percent of eggs will hatch, and fifty-four percent of the hatchlings will survive the first year.
lines.vis: Plain card: NT FIGURES, ON AVERAGE / Bar: 25% OF EGGS HATCH / Bar: 54% OF THOSE HATCHLINGS REACH YEAR 1 / Two measures stay separate, not merged

shots.vis: Plain card: NT FIGURES, ON AVERAGE; then Bar: 25% OF EGGS HATCH
Bar: 54% OF THOSE HATCHLINGS REACH YEAR 1

lines.card: NT FIGURES: 25% HATCH; 54% OF HATCHLINGS TO YEAR 1

shots.vis: Plain card on a dimmed background: 1% THOUGHT TO REACH MATURITY, IN THE WILD; then A hundred tiny silhouettes; one stays
Meter dips

lines.say: Hatchlings and juveniles can be eaten by barramundi, turtles, freshwater crocodiles and older saltwater crocodiles, and also by birds of prey and large fish. Very few make it to adulthood.
lines.vis: Quick, non-graphic silhouettes: a fish, a turtle, a larger crocodile / A bird of prey's shadow on the water / Back on one small hatchling in the crèche

shots.vis: Quick, non-graphic silhouettes: a fish, a turtle, a larger crocodile
A bird of prey's shadow on the water

shots.vis: Tile 3 flips half-way: the closing jaw again

lines.say: Number three. The bite.
lines.vis: Voiced number card over a closing jaw

shots.vis: Voiced number card over a closing jaw

lines.say: In one study, one saltwater crocodile produced a bite force of sixteen thousand four hundred fourteen newtons, about three thousand six hundred eighty-nine pounds.
lines.vis: A single adult saltwater crocodile on a plain field / The number 16,414 N slams in / Chip: ABOUT 3,689 LB / Chip: ONE ANIMAL, ONE STUDY

shots.vis: A single adult saltwater crocodile on a plain field; then The number 16,414 N slams in
Chip: ABOUT 3,689 LB
Chip: ONE ANIMAL, ONE STUDY

lines.say: The authors call this the highest bite force measured in any animal.
lines.vis: The number holds; a small crown icon / Meter ticks toward SWEET

shots.vis: The number holds; a small crown icon; then Meter ticks toward SWEET

lines.say: That value eclipses the highest recorded bite force in carnivoran mammals, four thousand five hundred newtons, about one thousand eleven pounds, in the spotted hyena.
lines.vis: A spotted hyena appears beside the crocodile / Two bars: 16,414 N and 4,500 N / Chip: 4,500 N, ABOUT 1,011 LB

shots.vis: A spotted hyena appears beside the crocodile
Two bars: 16,414 N and 4,500 N
Chip: 4,500 N, ABOUT 1,011 LB

lines.say: That sixteen thousand number is the top of a range, not the typical saltwater crocodile in the study.
lines.vis: The big 16,414 N shrinks to the top of a range bar / The bar is labelled a range, not an average

shots.vis: The big 16,414 N shrinks to the top of a range bar
The bar is labelled a range, not an average

lines.say: Seven adult saltwater crocodiles were tested. The representative bite force for the species was eight thousand nine hundred eighty-three newtons. The range was one thousand four hundred forty-six to sixteen thousand four hundred fourteen.

lines.say: Number four. The waterline.
lines.vis: Voiced number card over a still river edge

shots.vis: Voiced number card over a still river edge

lines.say: To capture prey, estuarine crocodiles wait in ambush at the water's edge, then lunge or snap sideways at animals that come to feed or drink.
lines.vis: A saltwater crocodile waits, almost still, at the edge / A wallaby steps in to drink / The crocodile lunges / snaps sideways (no long land chase)

shots.vis: A saltwater crocodile waits, almost still, at the edge
A wallaby steps in to drink
The crocodile lunges / snaps sideways (no long land chase)

lines.say: If they cannot swallow the animal whole, they may drag it under and twist it in a death-roll, or shake the head to break off pieces.
lines.vis: A drag under the surface / A tight death-roll, cut before gore / A head-shake, cut away

shots.vis: A drag under the surface
A tight death-roll, cut before gore
A head-shake, cut away

lines.say: Crocodiles usually hunt by staying submerged. They can stay unseen underwater for hours, and can attack from any depth, including very shallow water.
lines.vis: Underwater: a crocodile suspended, still / Hours tick on a faint clock, no fixed number / The same animal in water only centimetres deep

shots.vis: Underwater: a crocodile suspended, still
Hours tick on a faint clock, no fixed number
The same animal in water only centimetres deep

lines.say: They can attack in knee-deep water, so even wading can be dangerous.
lines.vis: A plain shot of knee-deep water at a bank / A crocodile outline under the surface / Card: EVEN WADING CAN BE DANGEROUS / Meter dips toward RAW

shots.vis: A plain shot of knee-deep water at a bank; then A crocodile outline under the surface; then Card: EVEN WADING CAN BE DANGEROUS; then Meter dips toward RAW

lines.say: Large saltwater crocodiles can stay underwater for up to one hour, because they can reduce their heart rate to two to three beats per minute.
lines.vis: A large crocodile sinks and waits / A heart icon slows to 2-3 beats per minute / Chip: UP TO ONE HOUR, FOR LARGE ANIMALS

shots.vis: A large crocodile sinks and waits
A heart icon slows to 2-3 beats per minute
Chip: UP TO ONE HOUR, FOR LARGE ANIMALS

lines.say: They use a minimum-exposure posture, with only the eyes, ears and nostrils above the water, so they often go unseen. If they are seen, it is hard to tell how big the crocodile is.
lines.vis: Only eyes, cranial platform, ears and nostrils break the surface / From the bank, the head looks small / Pull back: the body is much longer than it looked

shots.vis: Only eyes, cranial platform, ears and nostrils break the surface

shots.vis: Meatball in the bathtub, almost submerged; then Only the cardboard snout and eyes above the water

lines.say: When prey is detected, the crocodile makes a stealthy approach under water, then lunges rapidly and slams its jaws shut.

lines.say: Hunting starts almost as soon as they hatch. Full-grown adults can feed on whatever they can overpower, including other crocodiles.

lines.say: Females usually mature at about twelve years, and about two point three metres. Males mature in the mid-teens, at around three point three metres, depending on the official page.

lines.say: This species is considered the largest of the living crocodilians, with reported lengths of up to six to seven metres. Typical adults are smaller.

lines.say: The species is highly territorial, but they are known to congregate when resources are abundant. At Shady Camp lagoon on the Mary River, more than one hundred sub-adults and adults have been reported gathering when mullet spawn.

lines.say: As the number of large crocodiles rose after protection in 1971, the number of small ones fell. Small crocodiles are predated or excluded from rivers, and sometimes forced into marginal habitats, including upstream freshwater areas used for recreation.

lines.say: Although they are called saltwater crocodiles, they also live in freshwater.

lines.say: They can travel hundreds of kilometres in the water, especially after heavy rain and floods, and can be found in all types of waterways and the ocean.

lines.say: They can cross large stretches of open ocean, and they occur on islands up to ninety-six kilometres from the mainland.

lines.say: The species shows high site fidelity. Long-distance movements are usually linked to translocated adults, or to sub-adults looking for a territory. Some travel more than one hundred kilometres between breeding and non-breeding sites.

lines.say: They have a strong homing ability after being moved. In one Northern Territory study of problem crocodiles moved between river systems, recaptured animals found their way back a mean of twenty-five point six kilometres in a straight line, or sixty-five kilometres assuming a coastal return.

shots.vis: Voiced number card over a warning sign at a river

lines.say: Saltwater crocodiles are dangerous. They have attacked and killed people. They inhabit most areas of water in Kakadu National Park, including floodplains, freshwater billabongs, creeks, rivers and coastal areas.

lines.say: Always obey warning signs. If there are no warning signs, it is always best to assume crocodiles are present.

description:
What is life like for a saltwater crocodile? This is your whole life as one, from a seventy-gram hatchling in a vegetation mound to the waterline: 8 things you have to get through, then the verdict. Meatball tried all eight from the couch, with his dog, Noodle, as the stand-in and his cat, Sauce, as everybody else.

Checked facts in this video:
- Saltwater crocodile hatchlings are about 70 grams and about 30 centimetres long (Queensland Government).
- In Australian counts, females lay about 50 eggs, or 40 to 70. Incubation is typically 80 to 90 days, depending on temperature (IUCN Red List; Queensland Government).
- Nest temperature decides sex. On the Queensland page, 32°C produces both sexes but most are male; lower or higher temperatures produce more females; very high or very low temperatures kill the embryos (Queensland Government).
- The Australian Museum estimates that up to 75% of eggs laid in a season will not hatch, mostly from infertility, flooding, overheating, poor gas exchange and drying out, not predators.
- Northern Territory figures say, on average, only 25% of eggs will hatch and 54% of hatchlings will survive the first year. Only 1% of hatchlings are thought to survive to maturity in the wild (NT Government). The page is official but names no study and no count.
- In one study, one saltwater crocodile produced a bite force of 16,414 N (about 3,689 lb), the highest measured in any animal. Seven adult saltwater crocodiles were tested; the representative value for the species was 8,983 N (Erickson et al. 2012, PLoS ONE). Never read this as 'crocodiles bite at 3,689 pounds.'
- Estuarine crocodiles wait in ambush at the water's edge. They can attack in knee-deep water, so even wading can be dangerous (Queensland Government; Parks Australia, Kakadu). Large saltwater crocodiles can stay underwater for up to one hour (NT Government).
- Females usually mature at about 12 years; males in the mid-teens, depending on the official page (Queensland Government; NT Be Crocwise). Average adult length is 3–5 m (Australian Museum). The largest reliably measured animal, Mary River, 1974, was at least 615 cm (Australian Museum).
- IUCN lists Crocodylus porosus as Least Concern, with a stable trend. Queensland lists it as Vulnerable under state law. Those are different listings.
- Although they are called saltwater crocodiles, they also live in freshwater. They can travel hundreds of kilometres in the water, especially after heavy rain and floods. No waterway within their natural range can be considered crocodile-free (Queensland Be Crocwise).
- Safety, in areas where crocodiles live: keep out of the water; stay more than 5 metres away from the water's edge; be extra cautious at night, dusk and dawn (Queensland Be Crocwise). Never approach, interfere with or feed crocodiles, even small ones. Camp at least 50 metres from the water's edge. Any body of water in the Top End may contain large and potentially dangerous crocodiles (NT Be Crocwise). Saltwater crocodiles are dangerous. They have attacked and killed people. If there are no warning signs, assume crocodiles are present (Parks Australia, Kakadu). They can attack in knee-deep water, so even wading can be dangerous (Parks Australia, Kakadu).

General information, not safety advice for a specific place. Follow local warning signs and official Be Crocwise guidance.

Sources:
- Queensland Government, Estuarine crocodile: https://www.qld.gov.au/environment/plants-animals/animals/living-with/crocodiles/estuarine-crocodile
- Queensland Be Crocwise: https://www.qld.gov.au/environment/plants-animals/animals/living-with/crocodiles/becrocwise ; Be Crocwise top tips: https://www.qld.gov.au/environment/plants-animals/animals/living-with/crocodiles/becrocwise/be-crocwise-top-tips ; Where are crocs found: https://www.qld.gov.au/environment/plants-animals/animals/living-with/crocodiles/becrocwise/where-are-crocs-found
- IUCN Red List, Crocodylus porosus (errata version published in 2025), Webb et al. 2021, assessed 14 November 2019: https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/5668/268788998 ; assessment PDF: https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/5668/268788998/pdf
- Australian Museum, Estuarine Crocodile, Cecilie Beatson, updated 19/11/20: https://australian.museum/learn/animals/reptiles/estuarine-crocodile/
- NT Government, Crocodiles: https://nt.gov.au/environment/animals/wildlife-in-nt/crocodiles/crocodiles
- NT Be Crocwise, Saltwater crocodiles: https://becrocwise.nt.gov.au/about-crocodiles/saltwater-crocodiles ; Crocodiles and me: https://becrocwise.nt.gov.au/crocodiles-and-me ; home: https://becrocwise.nt.gov.au/
- Parks Australia, Kakadu, Staying safe: https://kakadu.gov.au/plan/plan-your-trip/staying-safe/
- Erickson GM et al. (2012) Insights into the ecology and evolutionary success of crocodilians revealed through bite-force and tooth-pressure experimentation. PLoS ONE 7(3): e31781. https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0031781
